title: Out-of-town labels coming to New Orleans after Imperial
summary: Reel four begins; Fats Domino's hits brought Imperial, but Deluxe, Apollo, Herald, Trumpet and Peacock had recorded in the city earlier.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: All right, reel number four, Cosmo Matanza, July 17th, 1993. Okay, we're going to continue on. No, we're going through the record companies, some of the early record companies that came to New Orleans, and we were talking about Imperial, Imperial Records. But Imperial would come here, and of course, with the first hits of Fats Domino, would of course have a long stay in New Orleans.

Yeah, well, I think Fats did something like 20 gold records in a row. Sure. It was phenomenal. But that, of course, opened the door for lots of other people, and it brought other people here, too. And you've got to remember now, Imperial wasn't the first company to come down. We talked about Deluxe and Apollo, and what was the guy in New Jersey had a label? I'm trying to think of it. You remember he did Walking with Mr. Lee?
That's Al Silvers. Yeah, but what time was his last name?
That was early enough recording Harold records. Somebody else I'm trying to think of.
Harold, Apollo. There were some other smaller New York labels.
Early on. And there were a couple of little labels out of, there was this one lady from Mississippi that came down and recorded. What's her name? She did blues things.
Trumpet records. Don Robey, Peacock records. I don't know.
